extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for reviewers on how to evaluate, write, discuss, and finalize reviews for ICLR 2024 submissions, including procedural deadlines, Code of Ethics reporting, and expectations for review content and conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timely and substantive reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Your reviews are timely and substantive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviews should be submitted within the conference deadlines and provide meaningful, detailed feedback rather than terse statements. Timeliness also includes participating in discussion phases and any scheduled borderline meetings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adherence to Code of Ethics and Code of Conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Read and adhere to the ICLR Code of Ethics; also adhere to the Code of Conduct in your role as a reviewer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All reviewers are required to read the Code of Ethics before starting reviews. As part of the review process, reviewers are asked to raise potential violations of the Code of Ethics. The Code applies to submission, reviewing, and discussion. Follow the Codes in reporting concerns and interacting with authors/reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete the CoE report when submitting review
rubrics_metrics.description: Complete the Code of Ethics (CoE) report: a form with two questions about potential CoE violations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The first question asks whether there is a potential violation of the CoE. The second is only relevant if there is a potential violation and asks the reviewer to explain why. Read the CoE before starting reviews so you can answer these questions accurately. To flag a CoE violation, indicate it on this form; the AC will work with PCs and the ethics board to resolve it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read the paper carefully and consult related work
rubrics_metrics.description: Carefully read through the entire paper and look up related work and citations that will help you comprehensively evaluate it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give yourself sufficient time to read. Supplementary material is optional but can often answer questions; consider it before asking authors. Be sure literature/context placement is assessed using relevant citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess the objective of the work
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine the goal of the paper: whether it addresses a known application/problem, highlights a new application/problem, introduces or explains a new theoretical finding, or some combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different objectives require different considerations of potential value and impact; tailor your evaluation to the stated objective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify strong points
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the submission is clear, technically correct, experimentally rigorous, reproducible, and presents novel findings (theoretical, algorithmic, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List the paper's strengths explicitly in the review so ACs and authors can see what works well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify weak points
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify weaknesses of the submission across clarity, correctness, experimental rigor, reproducibility, novelty, and other relevant aspects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be as comprehensive as possible. Distinguish minor issues from fundamental flaws that affect accept/reject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid biases and be open-minded
rubrics_metrics.description: Be mindful of potential biases and try to be open-minded about the value and interest a paper can hold for the entire ICLR community, even if not interesting to you personally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use objective criteria and consider broader impact and relevance; if in doubt consult with the area chair.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four key evaluative questions for recommendation
rubrics_metrics.description: Answer four key questions to make a recommendation: (1) What is the specific question/problem tackled? (2) Is the approach well motivated and well-placed in the literature? (3) Does the paper support the claims (correctness and scientific rigor)? (4) What is the significance of the work (new knowledge and value to community)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these four questions as the core of your assessment to recommend Accept or Reject. Consider rigor (theoretical and/or empirical), correctness, and significance; state how each question is resolved by the paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review organization and required elements
rubrics_metrics.description: When writing the initial review, organize it as: summarize what the paper claims; list strong and weak points; clearly state initial recommendation with one or two key reasons; provide supporting arguments; ask questions for authors; provide additional feedback to improve the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be positive and constructive in the summary. Make clear which feedback is essential for decision-making and which is for improving the paper. Provide 1–2 key reasons for your recommendation to aid AC decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide clear initial recommendation and reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Clearly state your initial recommendation (accept or reject) with one or two key reasons for this choice and provide supporting arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make it explicit which aspects led to your recommendation (e.g., technical correctness, novelty, missing experiments). This helps ACs and authors understand the decision rationale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask targeted questions for authors
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask questions you would like answered by the authors to clarify understanding and obtain additional evidence needed for confident assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Questions should be specific and aimed at resolving key uncertainties (e.g., assumptions, missing experimental details, proofs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide improvement-focused feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide additional feedback aimed to improve the paper; make clear these points are to help and not necessarily part of your decision assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate suggestions that would materially change acceptance from general suggestions for clarity, presentation, or future work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage actively in the discussion phase
rubrics_metrics.description: Be actively engaged during the asynchronous discussion phase; maintain openness to changing your initial recommendation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read other reviewers' feedback, respond to author replies, and be willing to revise your score upward or downward based on new information and clarifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attend or coordinate for borderline-paper meetings
rubrics_metrics.description: Area Chairs are required to meet with reviewers for all borderline cases; reviewers should attend or work with the AC to find a schedule that works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ACs will schedule one meeting per borderline paper. Reviewers agreed to participate when they accepted the invitation. An AC may downweight reviews from reviewers who refuse to attend (except emergencies). Familiarize yourself with other reviewers' feedback prior to the meeting for productive discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a final recommendation after discussion and revisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Update your review after the discussion phase (and any author revisions), state your final recommendation, and explain what did or didn’t change your recommendation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about how the discussion or revisions affected your view and whether outstanding concerns remain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process for flagging other policy violations
rubrics_metrics.description: To report other violations (plagiarism, double submission, paper length, formatting, etc.) contact the AC/SAC or the PC as appropriate via confidential comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use appropriate confidential channels and readership restrictions to raise these issues; AC will handle resolution with PC as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guidance on requesting additional experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: You may ask for additional experiments, but new experiments should not significantly change the content of the submission and should be limited in scope to more thoroughly validate existing results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requests for large new experiments that materially change the paper's claims are inappropriate; focus on experiments that address critical missing evidence needed for evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: State-of-the-art results are not required
rubrics_metrics.description: Lack of state-of-the-art (SOTA) results alone is not grounds for rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Papers provide value when they convincingly demonstrate new, relevant, impactful knowledge (empirical, theoretical, or practical), even without SOTA metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contemporaneous citation guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers published within the last four months prior to the deadline are considered contemporaneous; authors are not required to compare to peer-reviewed papers published within that window.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Since the full paper deadline was Sept 28, 2023, papers published on/after May 28, 2023 are considered contemporaneous. Authors are encouraged to cite relevant work but may be excused for not knowing very recent non-peer-reviewed (arXiv-only) papers. Reviewers should use judgment and consult AC if unsure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental and theoretical rigor expectations (from examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess experimental clarity and rigor (detailed protocols, baselines, tuning, number of runs, statistical significance) and theoretical soundness (clear statements of assumptions, proofs or evidence for claims, correct use of terminology).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example reviewer comments highlight missing experimental details (policy used, hyperparameters, number of runs, reward definitions), need to demonstrate statistical significance, clear assumptions for theoretical claims, and explicit proofs or explanations when claims about convergence/solutions are made. Ask authors for missing details and evidence where needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity, precision, and polish of the manuscript
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper should be written precisely and polished; imprecise or confusing exposition weakens the contribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point out unclear equations, inconsistent notation, ambiguous language, and suggest reorganization when sections are confusing. Minor writing issues should be separated from substantive logical or empirical flaws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer procedural tasks and timeline
rubrics_metrics.description: Main reviewer tasks and dates: create/update OpenReview profile, bid on papers, write and submit initial reviews, discuss with authors/other reviewers, flag CoE violations, provide recommendation to AC by deadline, participate in virtual meeting for borderline papers, provide final recommendation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the provided schedule (dates listed) and complete each step by the stated deadlines. These procedural requirements are part of reviewer obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone and conduct guidance for reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Be constructive, courteous, and helpful in reviews; adopt a spirit of openness and kindness when criticizing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See resources like Daniel Dennett's 'Criticising with Kindness' and similar guidance. Avoid hostile or dismissive language; focus on clear, actionable critique.
